longQuestions: Means of communications (post, telephone, mobile, internet, radio, TV) and transport (roads, railways, airways, shipping, pipelines) are the backbone of an economy.

Importance: (1) Expansion of markets — goods reach distant markets; (2) Development of agriculture — inputs reach farms and crops reach markets quickly; (3) Industrial growth — raw materials and finished goods are moved cheaply; (4) Large-scale production and division of labour; (5) Mobility of labour and capital.

(6) Price stability — goods move from surplus to deficit areas; (7) Growth of trade, both internal and foreign; (8) Employment in transport and telecom sectors; (9) Defence and national integration; (10) Spread of education, culture and information; (11) Help in emergencies and natural disasters; (12) Development of tourism and backward areas.
Pakistan Railways is the national railway (about 7,800 km of track), run by the Ministry of Railways; it carries passengers and goods across the country, linking Karachi port with the north.

Importance: cheap and safe transport for passengers and heavy goods (coal, wheat, oil, cement, fertiliser); links ports with industries and markets; provides employment to thousands; important for defence and national unity; saves fuel compared with road transport.

Performance: it has expanded and introduced new trains, dry ports and freight services, but suffers from losses, old locomotives and coaches, shortage of engines, delays, accidents, corruption and competition from road transport. Reforms such as new locomotives, track upgradation and CPEC's ML-1 project aim to improve it.
The computer and information technology (IT) means the use of computers, software, the internet and telecommunications to store, process and transmit information.

Importance: (1) Faster and accurate work in offices, banks and industries; (2) Banking — online banking, ATMs, mobile wallets; (3) E-commerce — buying and selling online; (4) Education — e-learning, online libraries; (5) Health — hospital records, telemedicine; (6) Communication — e-mail, social media, video calls.

(7) Employment and exports — software houses, freelancing and IT exports earn foreign exchange; (8) E-government — NADRA, online tax filing, e-challans; (9) Research and planning — data processing; (10) Industry — automation and design; (11) Agriculture — weather and market information. IT is thus essential for economic development.

The efficiency (productivity) of labour depends on: (1) Physical health and strength; (2) Mental ability and intelligence; (3) General and technical education and training; (4) Character — honesty, hard work and discipline; (5) Climate.

(6) Wages and incentives — good pay raises efficiency; (7) Working conditions — light, ventilation, safety and working hours; (8) Quality of machines, tools and raw materials; (9) Efficient organisation and management; (10) Job security and social security.
(11) Standard of living — food, housing, recreation; (12) Specialisation and division of labour; (13) Hope of promotion; (14) Peaceful industrial relations; (15) Political and economic stability.

Mobility of labour means the ability of workers to move from one place or occupation to another. Factors increasing it: (1) Education and technical training; (2) Better means of transport and communications; (3) Information about jobs (employment exchanges, internet, media).

(4) Higher wages and better facilities elsewhere; (5) Industrialisation and urbanisation creating new jobs; (6) Weakening of family ties and caste/social restrictions; (7) Peace and security; (8) Housing facilities in new places; (9) Opportunities of promotion; (10) Government policies encouraging migration (overseas employment).

(1) Low literacy and lack of technical skills; (2) Poor health and nutrition, lowering efficiency; (3) Unemployment and disguised unemployment, especially in rural areas; (4) Low wages and poor living standards; (5) Rapid growth of the labour force due to population growth.

(6) Child labour and exploitation; (7) Bad working conditions and lack of safety; (8) Weak trade unions and labour disputes; (9) Lack of social security, pensions and health insurance; (10) Immobility due to family ties and lack of information.
(11) Brain drain — skilled workers going abroad; (12) Low participation of women; (13) Insufficient training institutes; (14) Inflation reduces real wages; (15) Weak implementation of labour laws.

(1) Rapid population growth — the labour force grows faster than jobs; (2) Slow industrial growth and closure of factories due to energy shortages; (3) Mechanisation of agriculture reducing farm jobs; (4) Defective education system — degrees without skills; (5) Lack of technical and vocational training.

(6) Shortage of capital and low investment; (7) Political instability and law-and-order problems discourage investors; (8) Seasonal nature of agriculture; (9) Immobility of labour; (10) Return of workers from abroad; (11) Unequal distribution of land and wealth.
(12) Lack of employment planning; (13) Corruption and merit violations in jobs; (14) Low participation of the private sector; (15) Economic slowdown and inflation.

(1) Expansion of public sector development projects (roads, dams, CPEC); (2) Promotion of industries, special economic zones and SMEs through SMEDA; (3) Easy loans for youth — Prime Minister's Youth Loan Scheme, Kamyab Jawan Programme; (4) Microfinance and Khushhali Bank loans for self-employment.

(5) Technical and vocational training through TEVTA, NAVTTC and skill development programmes; (6) Overseas employment through the Bureau of Emigration and Overseas Employment; (7) Development of IT and freelancing; (8) Agricultural development and rural programmes; (9) Housing and construction schemes (Naya Pakistan Housing) which create jobs.

(10) Benazir Income Support Programme/Ehsaas for the poor; (11) Encouragement of foreign and private investment; (12) Employment quotas for women and the disabled; (13) Employment exchanges and job portals.
